title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Qilin and Sandworm are exploiting Cisco firewall management — root on the box that defines your plant boundary, and the federal deadline is tomorrow
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation. It is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and obtains root on the appliance operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then updated the advisory on 9 September to confirm it had seen exploitation in August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline. Cisco Talos attributes three clusters to this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: one dropping a web shell and a malicious JAR to steal credentials, one tied to the Russian state actor Sandworm deploying Cyclops Blink, and one linked to Qilin ransomware performing reconnaissance and building lists of endpoints to encrypt. The Qilin cluster is the one to brief your plant managers on. Enumerating encryption targets from the firewall management console is precisely how an IT intrusion becomes a stopped line, because FMC defines the boundary that is supposed to keep MES, historians and engineering workstations out of reach.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026

items.title: Panzer claims an Italian kitchen manufacturer — the detail worth your attention is the ESXi build, not the claim
items.content_text: Fresh analysis published on 10 September fills out the Panzer ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in August 2026 and has claimed victims in 11 countries in its first month. Two of the listed victims are Italian: kitchen manufacturer Doimo Cucine, posted on 17 August with roughly 30 GB of data claimed exfiltrated, and NTE Italia, a telecom engineering firm rather than a manufacturer, posted on 21 August with roughly 16 GB claimed. Neither company has confirmed an incident, researchers explicitly describe the listings as attacker claims rather than forensic proof, and no production halt has been confirmed at either. Treat the victim claims accordingly. What is worth acting on is the capability description: alongside Windows and Linux, Panzer ships builds for VMware ESXi and FreeBSD, and double extortion is standard. Hypervisor-level encryption is the part that lengthens industrial recovery, because in most plants the MES, historian, SCADA servers, batch and recipe management and the engineering-workstation images are virtual machines on a small number of ESXi hosts. Encrypt the hosts and every one of those goes at once, regardless of how well segmented the guests were from each other.
tags: Incident — Ransomware claim against a manufacturer, unconfirmed by the victim

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — Ransomware claim against a manufacturer, unconfirmed by the victim

items.title: Resolved: Boston Scientific says manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping are fully restored — and no manufacturing system was compromised
items.content_text: Boston Scientific announced on 9 September that manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping are “fully restored” and running at or above normal levels, closing out the cybersecurity incident it first identified on 25 August. Independent assessment by CrowdStrike and other third-party experts found no evidence of ongoing threat activity and no evidence that product development, manufacturing systems or cloud platforms were compromised; unauthorised access is assessed as having been limited to internal-facing IT infrastructure. Remote cardiac-device monitoring, which had also been disrupted, is likewise restored. The company has still not named an actor, confirmed ransomware, or disclosed root cause. This page previously carried the incident as an ongoing disruption with no recovery date; that framing is now superseded. The operational lesson survives the resolution intact, and it is the reason to keep the card on the board rather than the reason to panic: production stopped for roughly two weeks without anything published suggesting a controller, DCS or plant network was touched, because the systems that tell a factory what to build and where to ship it live on the IT side of the boundary.
tags: Incident — Resolved: IT compromise that had halted manufacturing and shipping

items.title: A phone call, not an exploit — McKesson’s SSO accounts were talked open, then used against Salesforce and Snowflake
items.content_text: McKesson disclosed on 31 August that it had discovered a cybersecurity incident on 25 August. The extortion group ShinyHunters claims responsibility, says it took roughly a terabyte over four days — about 284 million records — and demanded around $55 million; the company states it has not determined the incident to be material. The reported route in is the part worth studying: voice phishing against employees, leading to compromised Okta single sign-on accounts, and from there into the company’s Salesforce and Snowflake tenants. No software flaw was exploited. For a manufacturer the parallel is direct — MES, historian and quality data increasingly land in the same class of cloud analytics platform, reached with the same SSO, and the help desk that resets a plant engineer’s MFA is the same desk that was called here.
tags: Incident — Identity-based intrusion at a major distributor

items.title: A chip-programming supplier pulled its own production and shipping systems offline to contain ransomware
items.content_text: Data I/O, which builds the programming systems used to load firmware onto automotive and consumer electronics before assembly, detected ransomware on IT systems on 16 August and disclosed it in an 8-K filed with the SEC on 21 August. Containment involved taking systems offline, and the company said the outage affected shipping, manufacturing, production and support functions. More than 65% of its second-quarter business came from automotive electronics production. The point for a plant manager is second-order: this is a supplier whose downtime shows up as missing programmed parts on someone else’s line, and the disruption came from the containment decision as much as from the malware. The company has since said the incident was contained and systems restored.
tags: Incident — Ransomware, production and shipping systems taken offline

items.title: What a refusal to pay actually publishes: risk assessments, site documentation and plaintext credentials
items.content_text: Rhysida released the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set is around 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files, and beyond personnel and payroll records it is reported to include critical-infrastructure vulnerability analyses and plaintext credentials for administrator accounts and connected systems. Berlin’s own timeline is the operationally useful part: outflow first detected 7 August, continuing to around 12 August, with affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. For a manufacturer the read-across is direct. Your network diagrams, cell layouts, PLC program archives and OEM VPN credentials are rarely held in only one place — copies sit with machine builders, systems integrators, insurers and customers running supplier assurance, and a breach at any of them publishes your plant without touching your plant.
tags: Incident — Refusal to pay, then publication of infrastructure documentation

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — Refusal to pay, then publication of infrastructure documentation

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese scanning and relay platforms built out of other people’s IoT devices
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed intrusions through compromised routers and IoT devices so traffic appeared to come from ordinary domestic addresses. Both are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. Named victims are federal, but the relay design is the manufacturing lesson: unmanaged internet-connected devices in a plant — cameras, badge readers, HVAC controllers, machine-monitoring gateways — are exactly what these platforms recruited, and your firewall logs never showed who was really there.
tags: Incident — Law-enforcement action against state-sponsored infrastructure

items.title: Clop has named more than 40 PTC Windchill victims, and what it took is how your products are built
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations as victims of a campaign against internet-facing PTC Windchill product lifecycle management deployments, with manufacturing, aerospace and industrial suppliers among the confirmed names. Windchill is where design files, bills of material, supplier documentation, tolerances and change history live. Losing it is not a privacy incident. It is the disclosure of how a product is made, to whom it is sourced, and where the process is sensitive — and for firms whose competitive position rests on process knowledge rather than a patent, that is the whole asset. The campaign also demonstrates the pattern: attackers now go after the engineering record rather than the shop floor.

items.title: A credential-harvesting campaign built and executed by autonomous agents in under six hours
items.content_text: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group used an autonomous multi-agent framework to stand up and run a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours, with agents handling stages that used to take an operator days. GTIG separately observed actors targeting proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and co-opting victim cloud tenants to run their own workloads. Its guidance is to assume every threat actor is now using AI somewhere. For manufacturers the exposure is the credential layer around production: integrator and OEM support accounts, engineering-workstation logins, MES and ERP access, and the federated identity that increasingly sits behind vendor remote sessions into the cell.
tags: Threat intel — Autonomous agent frameworks in live intrusion operations

items.title: Deepfaked executives and suppliers are turning up in payment, procurement and change-request workflows
items.content_text: CYFIRMA reported on 2 September that deepfake-enabled social engineering impersonating executives and suppliers is becoming a practical operational and financial threat to manufacturing supply chains, showing up in payment authorisation, procurement and change-request workflows. The financial fraud version is well understood. The version that matters on this page is the operational one: a synthetic voice or video from a machine builder, maintenance contractor or OEM support engineer requesting an urgent remote session, a firmware file, a recipe change or an out-of-hours process adjustment — arriving through exactly the channels a genuine supplier uses. This is vendor research rather than a count of confirmed incidents, but it targets the entry path plants already rate as their weakest.
tags: Threat intel — Vendor research on deepfake-enabled supply-chain fraud

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat intel — Vendor research on deepfake-enabled supply-chain fraud
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CYFIRMA research reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor analysis, not incident data
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published and reported 2 Sep 2026

items.title: The way in is still somebody you already trust — contractor accounts and standing remote access top the entry-path list
items.content_text: Industrial Cyber reported on 4 September that the security firm F6 ranks manufacturing as the most-attacked sector in its 2026 telemetry, and says roughly 80% of the industrial organisations it works with — including designated critical-information-infrastructure facilities — are short of qualified security staff. The two entry paths it singles out are contractor compromise and trusted remote access: not exploits against the plant, but legitimate credentials belonging to somebody the plant already trusts. Its recommendations are operational rather than product-led — unified telemetry across IT and OT, the ability to reconstruct an intrusion chain quickly, alert correlation, and dedicated monitoring of contractor sessions as a distinct category. Two caveats: this is vendor-published data from one firm’s customer base, weighted toward its own region, so read the ranking as directional. The entry-path finding, though, matches what Dragos, CISA and this quarter’s integrator-compromise cases have reported independently.
tags: Threat intel — vendor telemetry on industrial attack volume and entry paths; contractor access and trusted remote access lead

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat intel — vendor telemetry on industrial attack volume and entry paths; contractor access and trusted remote access lead

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a plant the relevant figure is the gap between the enterprise perimeter and the engineering workstation — the same lateral path ransomware crews walk manually today, only faster.
tags: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect the plant — and a planning horizon of three months
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. Manufacturing is where the dependency map usually surprises people: MES scheduling, licence servers, recipe management, quality systems and label printing all sit on the enterprise side, so “cut IT and keep making product” frequently fails within a shift. That is the argument for pre-building separation points and testing them. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months of isolated operation is deliberately uncomfortable and worth using as a tabletop scenario rather than a target.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

items.title: An AI model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in hours — and bricked a third
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For a plant the uncomfortable part is the long tail: an exploit proven against one controller in a family is now cheaper to move onto the other variants sitting on your lines, which is exactly the population that never got patched because the CVE “did not apply to our model”.

items.title: Fire Ant hijacks the routers and authentication servers sitting between the plant and everything else
items.content_text: Sygnia’s 30 August research puts the China-nexus actor it calls Fire Ant inside network infrastructure rather than on top of it: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts across a large interconnected estate. Router implants suppressed selected syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and served interactive shells that produced no records; on TACACS the actor injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as logins were approved. Sygnia reports scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks but does not confirm compromise there. Most plants do not run IOS XR. Most plants do depend on a corporate network team, an integrator or an MSP for the routers and the authentication service between the enterprise and the cell — and on those same devices’ logs to prove what happened.

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. No victims, actors or techniques are named. For a plant the useful part is the instruction not to assume OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. In discrete and process manufacturing that usually means a specific short list: the machine an OEM ships with its own 4G router for remote support, the line acquired with a business unit and never brought under the standard build, the engineering workstation dual-homed for convenience, and the cell that still speaks Modbus or unauthenticated S7comm because the migration project was deferred. It lands the same week five US agencies described AI-written scripts reading S7 controllers across critical manufacturing.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: A ransomware affiliate ran an AI coding agent inside victim networks — and the exposed server shows exactly how
items.content_text: CloudSEK published analysis on 27 August of a misconfigured server belonging to a Russian-speaking Aurora ransomware affiliate, exposing tooling, command history, credential material and the operator’s Cursor chat transcripts. The campaign ran from April to July 2026 across nine countries; the operator reached domain-level or interactive access at 17 organisations, and four appeared on Aurora’s leak site. Manufacturing, food, agriculture and professional-services organisations were among those affected. The notable detail is not that AI was used but where: the transcripts show the assistant helping plan Active Directory escalation and intrusion steps, compressing the time between initial access and domain control. For a manufacturer the practical question is whether the identity used by IT administrators can reach the engineering workstations and the MES, because this operator’s route was domain privilege, not an ICS exploit.
tags: Threat Intel — Ransomware tradecraft, AI-assisted intrusion

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, with critical manufacturing named
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers in traffic resembling legitimate monitoring. Critical manufacturing is among the named sectors, and the agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than manipulation. The change worth internalising is not a new exploit. Writing a working S7 query used to require someone who knew the protocol; it no longer does, which enlarges the population capable of interrogating an exposed SIMATIC controller and makes obscurity a much weaker control than it was.
tags: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory naming critical manufacturing

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday hits the plant patch window — Siemens, Schneider and Aveva criticals, and one flaw already exploited
items.content_text: Siemens published seven advisories on 8 September, including critical fixes in Industrial Edge Management and Open Interface Services and a fourteen-CVE set for Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays led by an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8. Schneider Electric issued four the same day, headed by a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2, with PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert also patched. Aveva fixed four flaws in Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key. None of that is exploited. What is exploited is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a CVSS 10 pre-authentication remote code execution flaw added to KEV the same day — the remote-monitoring platform many MSP-managed plants inherit. Stacked on last week’s Rockwell batch, that is a lot of controller and engineering-workstation work chasing very few outage windows.
tags: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch batch, one chained item exploited

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth RCE in the remote-monitoring platform your MSP runs, plus two Windows zero-days
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog on 8 September. The one that reaches plants is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 giving unauthenticated remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against the platform’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and the vendor shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — a fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline is 11 September. Two Windows privilege-escalation zero-days were added the same day, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, along with CVE-2026-75650 in Adobe Commerce. N-central matters here because a managed-service console is a standing path onto engineering workstations at plants that outsource IT.
tags: Critical Advisory — Four actively exploited flaws added to CISA KEV

items.title: A malformed CIP message faults ControlLogix and CompactLogix controllers until someone power-cycles them
items.content_text: ICSA-26-244-03 covers CVE-2026-9637, an improper input-length validation flaw in CIP message processing rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 and CVSS v4.0 8.7. A crafted message drives ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380 controllers into a major non-recoverable fault, and recovery requires a physical power cycle — which on most lines means an unplanned stop and, for the GuardLogix families, a safety-function interruption. Rockwell has published fixed firmware. One point needs care: Rockwell’s own advisory header describes the issue as exploited, but SecurityWeek reports this is likely a documentation error, and CISA states it is unaware of exploitation. We report it as not known to be exploited, and would treat any contrary vendor confirmation as the trigger to escalate.
tags: Critical Advisory — Controller fault requiring a power cycle

items.title: A flaw in the OPC UA LocalDiscoveryServer — the component that tells every client where your servers are
items.content_text: CISA’s 3 September batch included ICSA-26-246-01, covering CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation’s UA LocalDiscoveryServer, with a fix in release 1.04.420. LDS is easy to overlook because nobody buys it: it arrives bundled inside OPC UA stacks and vendor products, and it is the component clients query to find out which servers exist and where. That makes it a quiet piece of plant-wide infrastructure — present on historian hosts, MES connectors, gateway appliances and OEM packages, usually installed by an integrator and rarely inventoried, let alone patched on any schedule. No exploitation has been reported.

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch is aimed at the engineering workstation — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September, and the theme is the engineering workstation rather than the controller. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client: CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — and that machine is usually the same laptop holding project files, licences and cell credentials. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH pushes firmware to Logix controllers and communication modules, so it habitually runs as an account with broad reach into the cell. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects. None is reported as exploited.
tags: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos

items.title: CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix controller fault flaw covered separately on this page (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them.

items.title: A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
items.content_text: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab.

items.title: A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
items.content_text: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. On a plant network this is the database under the historian, the MES, the batch or recipe store and the quality system — frequently an instance a machine builder or integrator installed as part of a line and left at the build it shipped with, sitting on the same flat network as the engineering workstations. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch.

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance runs as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre saw indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept appeared. In manufacturing, NetScaler routinely fronts the remote access used by engineers, third-shift support and the machine builders who dial in to diagnose equipment. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late.

items.title: The Git server holding your PLC projects just went into KEV — Gitea is being exploited in the wild
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. Rated CVSS 9.8, it lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July; exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea has become common in controls engineering because it is trivial to stand up inside a plant network for PLC projects, HMI screens, robot programs and configuration baselines. That convenience is the risk: a low-privilege contractor account converts into code execution on the machine holding the authoritative copy of your production logic. Federal remediation was due 28 August.

items.title: NIST finalises IR 8536 — a way to answer “where did this component actually come from?” without one central database
items.content_text: NIST has published the finalised version of IR 8536, a technology-neutral meta-framework for organising, linking and querying supply-chain traceability data across different systems and stakeholders without requiring a centralised repository. Its purpose is to let manufacturers assemble verifiable end-to-end provenance chains — raw material through fabrication, assembly, ship and receive — using interoperable event templates that different parties can each hold in their own systems. For supply-chain risk management that translates into two concrete questions becoming answerable: whether a component is counterfeit or substituted, and whether a piece of hardware or firmware entered the build without authorisation. This is standards guidance, not an advisory and not a response to an active threat; there is no CVE, no deadline and nothing to patch. It is worth a slot on a manufacturing board because component provenance is the control that sits underneath several of the threats already on this page — the PLM and engineering-data campaigns, and the integrator and machine-builder access paths that keep showing up as the way in.

items.title: 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the hours they take out of your response
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, using GAO figures, count 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of them applying to private industry. Their argument is operational: in the first hours of an incident the same handful of people is asked to satisfy several overlapping obligations on different clocks and in different formats, and that effort comes straight out of response. The timing matters because CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. Manufacturers are not lightly regulated here either — a multi-site producer can face CIRCIA, sector-specific rules for chemicals or defence work, state breach statutes, customer contractual notice clauses, and from 11 September the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s 24-hour reporting duty for its own products.

items.title: CISA and the G7 tell operators to start the post-quantum inventory now — the deadline is set by your asset lifetimes, not by them
items.content_text: CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group issued a joint call on 4 September for governments and organisations to begin the transition to post-quantum cryptography, setting out a phased, risk-based approach: inventory the cryptography in use and the dependencies that carry it, identify the data and systems whose exposure would outlast the migration, and hold a written transition plan rather than a procurement wish. The statement is explicit about store-now-decrypt-later — traffic captured today can be decrypted later — and about the second-order problem, which is that authentication and firmware-signing chains rest on the same public-key algorithms. It is guidance, not a rule, and no deadline attaches. For a plant the relevance is procurement: a controller or drive bought this year will still be in the line in the 2040s, and the signing and authentication cryptography baked into its firmware is decided by the vendor, not by you — unless you ask now.

items.title: OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical-infrastructure operators — terms not yet published
items.content_text: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For manufacturers the interesting part is the timing rather than the money: the same week produced Forescout’s demonstration that a supervised model can re-target a working PLC exploit at a sibling controller in hours, which is the offensive mirror of what this programme proposes to subsidise. Note it, wait for eligibility terms, and if you later evaluate it, treat it as you would any third party seeking telemetry from an engineering or plant network — because that is the data such tooling needs to be useful.

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and your customers will hold you to it
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates rather than legal boilerplate, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Manufacturers read this as a supplier, not as a victim: when an outage stops shipments, your customers’ production planning depends on how quickly and how honestly you can say what is affected and for how long. Boston Scientific’s late-August outage — which disrupted manufacturing, order processing and shipping — is the shape of the problem.

items.title: CISA publishes internet exposure reduction guidance — and the target list for this sector is engineering workstations, historian and MES bridges, OEM remote-support appliances on production machinery, and the cellular routers shipped inside packaged equipment
items.content_text: CISA released guidance on 26 August directing organisations to identify which of their systems are reachable from the internet, remove remote access that is not required, and harden whatever must stay externally accessible. It is deliberately unglamorous: an inventory step, a removal step and a hardening step, published in the same week the UK NCSC warned that internet-exposed OT and edge devices are being targeted with real-world disruption already caused. On a plant floor the exposure is rarely the PLC itself — it is the machine builder’s support appliance, the cellular router inside a packaged skid, or the historian bridge that was published so a corporate dashboard could reach it. Those arrive with the equipment and are commissioned by someone other than the security team. The guidance carries no deadline and applies to no one by force, which is precisely why it tends to be filed rather than executed.

items.title: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware — with a fuller report following. The obligation lands on the manufacturer, so it applies to industrial firms that build machinery, instruments or connected equipment as well as to software vendors. The practical difficulty is rarely the report itself; it is that a 24-hour clock requires a detection and decision path that most engineering organisations have never had to build.
